Text: This page describes exoplanet orbital and physical parameters. Most known extrasolar planet candidates have been discovered using indirect methods and therefore only some of their physical and orbital parameters can be determined. For example, out of the six independent parameters that define an orbit, the radial-velocity method can determine four: semi-major axis, eccentricity, longitude of periastron, and time of periastron. Two parameters remain unknown: inclination and longitude of the ascending node. There are exoplanets that are much closer to their parent star than any planet in the Solar System is to the Sun, and there are also exoplanets that are much further from their star.

Physical parameters, often inferred from observations, encompass mass, radius, density, surface temperature, and atmospheric composition. Density, calculated from mass and radius, offers clues about a planet's internal structure (rocky, gaseous, etc.). Atmospheric studies, using spectroscopy, unveil the presence of gases and potentially biosignatures. Together, these orbital and physical parameters paint a picture of an exoplanet's environment and evolutionary history.

Text: Antigenic drift is a kind of genetic variation in viruses, arising from the accumulation of mutations in the virus genes that code for virus-surface proteins that host antibodies recognize. This results in a new strain of virus particles that is not effectively inhibited by the antibodies that prevented infection by previous strains. This makes it easier for the changed virus to spread throughout a partially immune population. Antigenic drift occurs in both influenza A and influenza B viruses. (Confusion can arise with two very similar terms, antigenic shift and genetic drift.

Text: Antigenic drift is a gradual process of change in the antigens of a pathogen, like influenza viruses. It arises from the accumulation of small genetic mutations during viral replication. These mutations alter the virus's surface proteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), making it less recognizable to the immune system. Consequently, previously effective antibodies are less capable of neutralizing the drifted virus, leading to reduced vaccine efficacy and the potential for repeated infections. The continuous, minor changes facilitated by antigenic drift are a major driver of seasonal influenza epidemics, necessitating yearly vaccine updates to target the most prevalent circulating strains.

Text: Fluid motion involves angular momentum, a measure of rotational inertia. In inviscid (frictionless) fluids, conservation of angular momentum dictates that vorticity, the local rotation of fluid elements, remains constant following the fluid. However, real fluids have viscosity, leading to viscous diffusion of vorticity, smoothing out rotational variations. The interplay between these effects governs the overall flow behavior. For example, boundary layers, regions near solid surfaces, experience significant angular momentum changes due to no-slip conditions, creating complex swirling patterns. Understanding angular momentum transport is crucial for modeling turbulent flows and analyzing phenomena like tornadoes or the dynamics of rotating machinery within fluids.

Text: The substitution model describes how a solute dissolves in a solvent. Imagine the solvent molecules surrounding a solute particle. The rate of substitution depends on factors like temperature, solute-solvent interactions, and the solute's surface area. Stronger interactions lead to higher solubility, while increased temperature often accelerates dissolution. Essentially, the substitution model explains how a homogeneous solution forms at a molecular level through the progressive replacement of solute-solute interactions with solvent-solute interactions.

A high level of S–R compatibility is typically associated with a shorter reaction time, whereas a low level of S-R compatibility tends to result in a longer reaction time, a phenomenon known as the Simon effect. The term "stimulus-response compatibility" was first coined by Arnold Small in a presentation in 1951.

This includes animal communication, plant signaling, and the broader flow of information across biotic and abiotic realms. By analyzing the "texts" of nature – from animal tracks to weather patterns – ecosemiotics unveils the intricate webs of meaning driving ecological dynamics, revealing how meaning-making is fundamental to ecological processes and sustainability.  This interdisciplinary field bridges biology, semiotics, and ecology, offering new perspectives on environmental issues and conservation efforts.

Text: Dorsal pancreatic agenesis is a rare congenital anomaly characterized by the incomplete or absent development of the dorsal pancreas, one of the two embryonic pancreatic buds.  This usually affects the tail and body of the pancreas, potentially leading to variations in pancreatic size and shape.  While often asymptomatic,  individuals may experience mild digestive issues like malabsorption or diabetes due to insufficient insulin production.  Diagnosis typically involves imaging studies like ultrasound or CT scans, revealing a smaller-than-normal pancreas or absence of the dorsal component.  Treatment focuses on managing any associated symptoms, often involving dietary modifications or medication.  The condition's severity varies greatly, ranging from clinically insignificant to requiring significant medical intervention.

Text: In deep learning, fine-tuning is an approach to transfer learning in which the parameters of a pre-trained neural network model are trained on new data.[1] Fine-tuning can be done on the entire neural network, or on only a subset of its layers, in which case the layers that are not being fine-tuned are "frozen" (i.e., not changed during backpropagation).[2] A model may also be augmented with "adapters" that consist of far fewer parameters than the original model, and fine-tuned in a parameter-efficient way by tuning the weights of the adapters and leaving the rest of the model's weights frozen.

Text: Fine-tuning in deep learning adapts a pre-trained model to a specific task.  Instead of training a model from scratch, which requires vast data and resources, fine-tuning leverages a model already proficient in a related domain.  This involves adjusting the pre-trained model's weights using a smaller, task-specific dataset.  This approach is significantly faster and often requires less data than training from scratch.  The pre-trained model's learned features serve as a strong foundation, accelerating the learning process and yielding improved performance, particularly when data is limited.  Fine-tuning is crucial for efficiently tackling diverse applications, ranging from image recognition to natural language processing.

Text: Equivalent weight in a fluid signifies the weight of a fluid displaced by a submerged or floating object.  Archimedes' principle directly relates this concept to buoyancy.  The upward buoyant force acting on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.  Therefore, an object's equivalent weight is the difference between its actual weight and the buoyant force.  If the equivalent weight is positive, the object sinks; if it's zero, the object floats neutrally; and if negative, the object rises.  This principle is crucial in determining the stability and behavior of submerged and floating bodies, influencing fields like naval architecture and hydrostatics.  Density differences between the object and fluid are key determinants of equivalent weight.

Text: In engineering, a bug is a design defect in an engineered system that causes an undesired result. Although used exclusively to describe a technical issue, bug is a non-technical term; applicable without technical understanding of the system. The term bug applies exclusively to a system that is (human) designed; not to a natural system; and that the issue is within the influence of human control. For example, humans have faults but not bugs, and a server crash due to natural disaster is not a bug. In addition to or instead of defect, some use: error, flaw or fault.

Root cause analysis often involves examining design flaws, manufacturing defects, operational issues, or external factors influencing the fluid's behavior. Effective debugging requires careful observation, data analysis, and potentially iterative design modifications to ensure the system operates as intended, safely and efficiently.

Text: Hydrothermal vents, underwater volcanic fissures, support unique microbial ecosystems.  These communities thrive in extreme conditions, fueled by chemosynthesis rather than sunlight.  Bacteria and archaea dominate, utilizing chemicals like hydrogen sulfide and methane from vent fluids for energy.  This primary production supports a complex food web, including specialized invertebrates and other microorganisms.  Vent microbial communities exhibit remarkable adaptation to high temperatures, pressure, and toxic chemicals.  Their metabolic diversity is a crucial area of research, revealing potential for biotechnological applications and insights into early life on Earth.  Studying these ecosystems expands our understanding of life's limits and adaptability.

Text: Photopharmacology harnesses light to control drug activity.  It involves designing molecules, termed photopharmaceuticals, whose biological function is switched on or off by specific wavelengths of light. This offers precise temporal and spatial control over drug action, surpassing traditional approaches.  Applications include targeted drug delivery, improved therapeutic efficacy, and reduced side effects.  For example, a photopharmaceutical could be inactive until illuminated at a specific site within the body, thereby minimizing off-target effects. This emerging field holds immense potential for advancing various therapeutic areas, especially in oncology and neuroscience.

Text: The exosporium is the outer surface layer of mature spores. In plant spores it is also referred to as the exine. Some bacteria also produce endospores with an exosporium, of which the most commonly studied are Bacillus species, particularly Bacillus cereus and the anthrax-causing bacterium Bacillus anthracis. The exosporium is the portion of the spore that interacts with the environment or host organism, and may contain spore antigens.[1] Exosporium proteins, such as Cot protein, are also discovered related to strains of B. anthracis and B.cereus. This Cot protein share similar sequences with other spore coat proteins, and their putative determinants are believed to include bxpC, lunA, exsA, etc.

Text: The exosporium is a thin, outermost layer found in some bacterial endospores. Its presence varies widely among bacterial species;  some spores possess a well-defined exosporium, while others lack it entirely.  The composition and structure of the exosporium can contribute to the unique properties and resilience of particular endospore types.  Research continues to illuminate the complexities of this intriguing outermost spore layer.

Text: Historical ecology is a research program that focuses on the interactions between humans and their environment over long-term periods of time, typically over the course of centuries.[1] In order to carry out this work, historical ecologists synthesize long-series data collected by practitioners in diverse fields.[2] Rather than concentrating on one specific event, historical ecology aims to study and understand this interaction across both time and space in order to gain a full understanding of its cumulative effects. Through this interplay, humans both adapt to and shape the environment, continuously contributing to landscape transformation.

Text: Assimilative capacity refers to an environment's ability to absorb a pollutant or waste without suffering significant negative impacts.  This capacity is not infinite; exceeding it leads to ecological damage.  Factors determining assimilative capacity include the pollutant's characteristics (toxicity, persistence), the environment's physical attributes (size, flow rate, temperature), and the presence of natural processes that break down or dilute the contaminant (e.g., microbial activity, dilution).  Understanding assimilative capacity is crucial for sustainable resource management and pollution control, guiding decisions on waste discharge limits and environmental protection strategies.  It helps determine safe levels of pollution, preventing irreversible harm to ecosystems.

Text: Amoebas, single-celled organisms, exhibit fascinating movement and feeding behaviors within fluid environments.  They utilize pseudopodia, temporary extensions of their cytoplasm, for locomotion and engulfing food through a process called phagocytosis.  The fluid's viscosity significantly impacts amoeboid movement;  higher viscosity creates resistance, slowing pseudopod extension.  Conversely, lower viscosity allows for more rapid movement.  Osmosis, the movement of water across the cell membrane, also plays a crucial role, maintaining the amoeba's internal water balance and preventing lysis (bursting) in hypotonic solutions.  The interaction between the amoeba and its fluid environment is a dynamic interplay of physical forces and biological processes essential for survival.

Text: In geology, provenance refers to the origin of sedimentary rocks and their constituent clasts (fragments). Determining provenance involves tracing the source of sediments back to their parent rocks.  Analysis techniques include examining the clasts' mineralogy, geochemistry, and roundness, as well as studying the overall sedimentary structure.  This reveals information about the source area's lithology, tectonic setting, and weathering history.  Provenance studies are crucial for understanding landscape evolution, sediment transport mechanisms, and basin formation. Reconstructing the provenance allows geologists to build a comprehensive picture of past geological processes and environments.

Text: Particle deposition describes the process where suspended particles in a fluid, like a gas or liquid, adhere to a surface.  This occurs due to various mechanisms, including Brownian diffusion (random motion of small particles), gravitational settling (larger particles succumb to gravity), inertial impaction (particles' inertia carries them towards the surface), and interception (particles contacting a surface due to their size).  The deposition rate depends on particle properties (size, shape, density), fluid properties (velocity, viscosity), and surface characteristics (roughness, wettability). Understanding particle deposition is crucial in many fields, including air pollution control, aerosol science, and biomedical engineering, impacting areas such as lung health, filter design, and material synthesis.

Text: ASR-completeness, in the context of automated speech recognition (ASR), signifies a system's ability to accurately transcribe any spoken utterance within a defined linguistic domain. Achieving this requires robust acoustic modeling, language modeling, and sophisticated handling of out-of-vocabulary words and noisy audio. In particular, three data sets are commonly used in different stages of the creation of the model: training, validation, and test sets. The model is initially fit on a training data set,[3] which is a set of examples used to fit the parameters (e.g. weights of connections between neurons in artificial neural networks) of the model.

Text: Machine learning models learn from data.  To prevent overfitting – where a model memorizes the training data instead of learning generalizable patterns – we use three distinct datasets.  The training set teaches the model; it's the bulk of the data.  The validation set guides model selection and hyperparameter tuning, preventing overfitting to the training data by providing an unbiased evaluation during development. Finally, the test set provides an objective, final evaluation of the trained model's performance on unseen data, representing how well it generalizes to real-world scenarios.  Properly splitting data into these sets is crucial for building robust and reliable models.

Text: Seismic velocity in a fluid, unlike solids, depends solely on its bulk modulus (resistance to compression) and density.  Shear waves cannot propagate through fluids because they lack the necessary shear strength; any applied shear stress is immediately dissipated.  Consequently, only compressional (P) waves travel, with velocity determined by the square root of the bulk modulus divided by density.  Variations in these properties, such as temperature or salinity changes in water, directly affect the P-wave velocity.  Higher bulk modulus or lower density leads to faster wave propagation.  Studying these velocities provides crucial insights into fluid properties and subsurface structures containing fluids, like reservoirs or aquifers.
Label: AI
